### What happened
This benchmark evaluated the performance of spectral feature extraction on 10,000 sensor records, comparing a single-threaded baseline against a 4-worker parallel configuration. Each record consisted of a 16-sample window processed to identify anomalies. The single-threaded run recorded a wall time of 480.3 ms, while the multi-threaded run completed in 249.0 ms. Structural validation was successful, as both runs produced an identical checksum of 831583345 and identified 1830 anomalies. Because the results are equal, the comparison is considered valid. These are user-device measurements that are structurally validated but not server-attested.

### Why it happened
The observed speedup of 1.93x resulted from partitioning the 10,000 records into four discrete chunks of 2,500 records each. In this architecture, Web Workers operate with isolated memory, relying on message passing rather than shared mutable data. The wall time includes the entire thread lifecycle: worker creation, module loading, data copying, transfer, coordination, and receiving results. While the single-threaded compute time was 262.4 ms, the individual parallel workers completed their tasks in approximately 64.6 ms to 67.1 ms. 

The difference between the total wall time and the maximum worker compute time represents the non-kernel elapsed time, which includes the overhead of scheduling and communication. It is important to note that the baseline ran first; therefore, cache states, JIT compilation, and general system activity may bias the results. No specific claims are made regarding the number of physical cores, CPU utilization, or the underlying OS scheduling policy.

### In an AI pipeline
In a production AI pipeline, this type of multithreading is utilized for parallel AI feature preprocessing rather than model training. Before sensor data can be fed into a neural network, it must be transformed into spectral features. By distributing 16-sample sensor windows across multiple workers, the system reduces the latency required to prepare data for inference. This ensures that the preprocessing stage does not become a bottleneck, even when accounting for the overhead of transferring data between the main thread and isolated worker contexts. This measurement reflects the actual time a user’s device spends coordinating these tasks.
